assistant|checklist_pre_contract_documen: Pre-contract documents for a home purchase: purchase agreement, pre-approval letter, and proof of funds
assistant|checklist_due_diligence_docume: Due diligence documents: home inspection report, appraisal report, title search and insurance, and environmental reports
assistant|checklist_loan_documents: Loan documents: mortgage application, loan estimate, final loan disclosure, and mortgage note
assistant|checklist_insurance_documents: Insurance and warranty documents: homeowners insurance policy and manufacturer warranty documents
assistant|checklist_closing_documents: Closing documents: closing disclosure, deed, title, bill of sale, and closing statement
assistant|checklist_other_documents: Other documents needed: government-issued identification, proof of income (pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns), and recent bank statements
assistant|timeline_pre_contract: Before making an offer, obtain the pre-approval letter from the lender and gather proof of funds for the down payment and closing costs
assistant|timeline_contract_stage: After making an offer, sign the purchase agreement and provide earnest money, typically 1-2% of the purchase price
assistant|timeline_due_diligence: Due diligence documents (home inspection, appraisal, title search and insurance, environmental reports) are handled 1-2 weeks after contract signing
assistant|timeline_loan_processing: Loan application and processing (mortgage application, loan estimate, final loan disclosure) occur 2-4 weeks after contract signing
assistant|timeline_insurance_warranty: Homeowners insurance policy and warranty documents are arranged 2-4 weeks after contract signing
assistant|timeline_closing_preparations: Closing preparations (closing disclosure, ID, proof of income, bank statements) happen 1-2 weeks before closing
assistant|timeline_closing_final: At closing, the deed and bill of sale are signed, title is received, the closing statement is reviewed, and the loan is funded
assistant|common_inspection_issues: Common home inspection issues include roofing/gutters, plumbing leaks and corroded pipes, faulty wiring, foundation cracks, HVAC and insulation problems, pest infestation, environmental concerns, and malfunctioning appliances
assistant|inspection_negotiation_options: Using the inspection report, a buyer can request repairs, request credits at closing, renegotiate the price, or walk away from the contract
assistant|inspection_negotiation_tips: Tips for negotiating with the seller: prioritize critical issues, provide evidence from the report, be reasonable, get everything in writing, and consult a professional
assistant|seller_repair_follow_through: To ensure the seller follows through on repairs, get the agreement in writing, specify the scope of work, set a deadline before closing, hold back funds in escrow, verify repairs at a final walk-through, request a lien release, and keep records
assistant|third_party_contractor_benefit: A third-party contractor reviewing repairs provides an independent evaluation, specialized expertise, verification of completeness, additional negotiating power, and documentation of the property's condition at sale
assistant|contractor_selection_tips: When selecting a third-party contractor, get referrals, check that they are licensed and insured, request a written report, and insist on a neutral party with no affiliation to the seller
assistant|final_appraisal_practice: Getting a second appraisal before closing is not common practice but not unheard of; an initial appraisal is usually valid for 30 to 60 days
assistant|final_appraisal_when_to_consid: A final appraisal before closing may be worth considering if the property changed significantly, the local market fluctuated, or there are concerns about the initial appraisal's accuracy
assistant|final_appraisal_steps: If getting a final appraisal, notify the lender, choose a different appraiser for independence, and carefully review and understand the report
